source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter I, §4 Some Winning Positions in the Middle-game, Example 15

steps.title: A very frequent combination
steps.source: A very frequent type of combination is shown in the following position. Here White is the exchange and a Pawn behind, but he can win quickly.

narration.say: A very frequent type of combination.
White is the exchange and a pawn behind. But look at the bishop on d3, aiming at h7.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Sacrifice the bishop with check.

feedback.*: The bishop takes the pawn in front of the king.

narration.say: Now bring the queen with check.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Check with the queen.

feedback.*: The queen checks on the h-file.

exercise.success: 2. Qh5, check. Black goes back to g8.

steps.title: Your turn: the knight joins
steps.source: 3 Kt - Kt 5, and Black cannot stop mate at K R 7 except by sacrificing the Queen by Q - K 5, which would leave White with a Q for a R.

narration.say: Queen on h5. One more piece, and h7 falls.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Bring the knight to support the queen.

feedback.*: The knight goes where it supports h7.

exercise.success: 3. Ng5. Black cannot stop mate on h7, except by giving up his queen with Qe4.

narration.say: White now has a queen against a rook, and should win easily.

steps.title: If Black does not take
steps.source: (If 1…K - R 1; 2 Q - K R 5, P - K Kt 3; 3 Q - R 6, and wins.)

narration.say: And if Black does not take the bishop?
King to h8. Then queen to h5.
Black blocks with g6, and queen to h6 wins.
Bishop takes h7 check, queen to h5 check, knight to g5: remember this pattern.
It works when the bishop, queen and knight can all reach the king's side quickly.
